slides.headline: This fish walks out of water. On its fins.
slides.sub: Meet the mudskippers of the genus Periophthalmus

slides.headline: A fish of the mudflats
slides.body: Mudskippers are gobies of swamps, estuaries and tidal mud, from Africa across the Indo-Pacific to Australia. They climb, walk and skip about out of water.

slides.headline: It walks on crutches
slides.body: Both pectoral fins move together, lifting and vaulting the front half of the body forward onto the pelvic fins. Scientists call this gait 'crutching'.

slides.headline: Breathing without water
slides.body: On land it breathes through its skin and air held in its gill chambers. The Atlantic mudskipper also holds water and air in its mouth.

slides.headline: A fish that blinks
slides.body: Mudskippers evolved blinking on their own. The Atlantic mudskipper retracts its eyes to blink, and blinks more often in drying air to keep them wet.

slides.headline: Save this for your next mangrove walk.
slides.body: One strange animal at a time, sources included. Follow @earthspirit_nature.

caption:
Mudskippers (genus Periophthalmus) are fish that climb, walk and skip about out of water, using their fins as crutches.

These amphibious gobies hunt crustaceans and other small animals on the mud.

Swipe for the full story. Sources on the last slide.

Source: Britannica; Aiello et al. (2023) PNAS.
